adaptation: The edit itself is the 3.4.y backport's edit (cd34de10471a5ddad397739fae33555d47e53769): the cast goes on the first operand of the nanosecond sum, so every addition is 64-bit. The only difference is the leading whitespace -- this tree's call is wrapped one level deeper, so the line carries three tabs where the stable branch's carries two, and the earlier claim here that the line was "byte-identical" was therefore not exact (Codex 2026-10-31). What is identical is the expression and the change to it. Nothing is compensated for, no constant is subtracted, and no code path is special-cased. The v3.6 commit listed above (ec145babe754f9ea1079034a108104b6001e001c) is the fix upstream, but it is not the same edit: it removes the same overflow by giving the function an s64 nanosecond accumulator and timespec_add_ns(). The stable backport is the one this tree takes, because it is the change this tree's own line can carry.
why: get_monotonic_boottime() adds three timespec nanosecond fields, each a signed 32-bit long on this ARM32 target, before the s64 term joins them. Three normalised fields can sum past 2147483647, and the 32-bit result is then sign-extended into the 64-bit value, so CLOCK_BOOTTIME comes back short by exactly 2^32 ns (4.294967296 s). Two fields cannot do it (at most 1999999998), which is why the two-field sums at line 250 (in ktime_get(), not getnstimeofday() as this file said until it was checked), getboottime() at line 964 and line 1069 are unaffected and are left alone; line 999 is the only three-field sum in kernel/ and fs/proc/ in this tree. Before any suspend total_sleep_time is zero, so the sum stays under the threshold and the fault cannot appear -- which is why it shows up against lid-switch sleeps. /proc/uptime reaches the same clock through monotonic_to_bootbased() and timespec_add(), normalising in steps, so a wall-clock-against-/proc/uptime measurement does not see this and cannot be used to clear it.
